body.head: SIX RESERVED LEGAL ACTIVITIES (LSA 2007)

body: ALTERNATIVE BUSINESS STRUCTURES (ABS): An ABS allows non-lawyers to own or manage legal services businesses. Must be licensed by an approved regulator (e.g. the SRA). Not available for firms where a non-lawyer holds a material interest and is not approved.

REFERRAL FEES — PERSONAL INJURY: Referral fees in personal injury cases are prohibited (ss.56-60 Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012). It is a criminal offence to pay or receive a referral fee for a PI referral. Applies to claims management companies, insurers and solicitors.

REGULATORY OBJECTIVES (LSA 2007, s.1): The eight regulatory objectives include: protecting and promoting the public interest; supporting the constitutional principle of the rule of law; improving access to justice; protecting and promoting the interests of consumers; promoting competition in the provision of legal services.

LEGAL OMBUDSMAN: Deals with complaints from consumers of legal services. Solicitors must signpost the Ombudsman in their complaints procedure. The Ombudsman can award compensation up to £50,000 and direct remedial action.

REGULATED PROFESSION = RESERVED LEGAL ACTIVITIES: Under the Legal Services Act 2007, being a member of a regulated profession means you are authorised to undertake RESERVED LEGAL ACTIVITIES (rights of audience, litigation, conveyancing, probate, notarial activities, oaths). This is the specific legal meaning — not merely 'must abide by rules' (too generic) or 'has specific rights' (incomplete). See 10.1.3.1.

11.8.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: EU LAW — PAST TENSE: Since Brexit (31 Jan 2020), the UK is NO LONGER a member of the EU. EU law no longer has direct effect or supremacy in the UK. Questions about EU law in SQE1 context relate to historical or comparative constitutional law, or the RETAINED EU law position.

RETAINED EU LAW: Post-Brexit, EU-derived law still applies in the UK as 'retained EU law' unless repealed or modified. It is NOT EU law — it is UK law that originated from the EU. Parliament can repeal or amend it.

FACTORTAME — HISTORICAL: Factortame established that UK courts could disapply Acts of Parliament inconsistent with directly effective EU law. This power was based on ECA 1972 and no longer applies. Parliamentary sovereignty is now unqualified in UK domestic law.

11.7.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: s.3 vs s.4 HRA: s.3 — court reads legislation compatibly with Convention rights (does NOT invalidate legislation; remains fully in force but interpreted differently). s.4 — court issues declaration of incompatibility (legislation STILL in force; Parliament must change it; the claimant gets NO direct remedy from the declaration).

ABSOLUTE vs QUALIFIED RIGHTS: Articles 2, 3 (core), 4(1), 7 are absolute — no justification possible for interference. Articles 8, 9, 10, 11 are QUALIFIED — interference permitted if prescribed by law, legitimate aim, proportionate. Art 5 and 6 are 'limited' — specific exceptions permitted.

PUBLIC AUTHORITY — s.6: Public authorities must act compatibly. A purely PRIVATE body is NOT bound by the HRA (though courts as public authorities must apply Convention-compatible common law). The question of whether a private body performing public functions is a 'public authority' is fact-specific and often tested.

s.7 — VICTIM STANDING: Unlike JR (sufficient interest), HRA claims require the claimant to be a VICTIM. Pressure groups, NGOs and third parties who are not directly affected CANNOT bring HRA claims in their own name (though they may intervene in other proceedings).

11.6.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: THREE GROUNDS — NOT A CLOSED LIST: The CCSU three grounds are analytical categories — 'legitimate expectation' is a subcategory of illegality/procedural impropriety, not a separate ground. A substantive legitimate expectation can also give rise to a substantive remedy.

WEDNESBURY vs PROPORTIONALITY: Wednesbury applies to ordinary domestic law JR (not HRA). Proportionality applies where Convention rights are engaged — it is a more intensive standard. The two standards are NOT the same — a proportionality analysis involves four stages; Wednesbury is a 'very high' threshold of unreasonableness.

PERMISSION — PROMPTLY: The 3-month time limit runs from the date the GROUNDS AROSE, not from when the claimant learned of the decision. 'Promptly' means as soon as practicable — permission can be refused even within 3 months if delay causes prejudice.

PUBLIC BODY — PUBLIC FUNCTION: JR only available against bodies exercising PUBLIC functions. Private bodies (even if large — e.g. Jockey Club) may not be amenable to JR unless performing a public function (R v Panel on Takeovers ex p Datafin [1987]).

11.5.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: RIOT vs VIOLENT DISORDER: Riot requires 12+ persons; violent disorder requires only 3+. Both require use OR threat of violence — you do not need to prove each individual used violence, only that the group collectively did.

s.5 — NO INTENT REQUIRED: Unlike s.4A (which requires INTENT to cause harassment etc.), s.5 only requires that the behaviour is of a type that a person likely to be present would find harassing/alarming/distressing. The defendant need not intend the effect.

AFFRAY — 'PERSON OF REASONABLE FIRMNESS': The person of reasonable firmness need not actually be present — the test is objective (hypothetical bystander). The actual victim does not have to be 'of reasonable firmness'.

11.4.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: SEPARATION OF POWERS — UK IS NOT STRICT: The UK does NOT have a strict separation. The executive sits in the legislature (ministers in Parliament). The Lord Chancellor was historically in all three branches. Do not apply US-style separation to UK questions.

RULE OF LAW vs PARLIAMENTARY SOVEREIGNTY: These can conflict. Parliament can pass laws that undermine rule of law principles (e.g. retrospective legislation, ouster clauses). Courts interpret statutes to minimise conflicts with rule of law (principle of legality — R v SoS ex p Simms [2000]). But if Parliament uses sufficiently clear words, courts must give effect to the statute.

JUDICIAL REVIEW vs APPEAL: Judicial review is NOT an appeal. JR challenges the LEGALITY of a decision, not its merits (unless human rights engaged, where proportionality applies). The court will not substitute its own view for that of the decision-maker on questions of merit/policy.

CRA 2005 CHANGES: The Supreme Court replaced the APPELLATE COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS (not the House of Lords itself) as the highest court. Law Lords became Justices of the Supreme Court. The Lord Chancellor no longer sits as a judge or Speaker of the Lords.

11.3.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: PARLIAMENTARY SOVEREIGNTY: Parliament can legislate on ANYTHING — there is no entrenched constitution and courts cannot strike down primary legislation (unlike the US Supreme Court).

PREROGATIVE vs STATUTE: where Parliament has legislated, the prerogative is displaced to the extent of the statute (De Keyser [1920]). You cannot use prerogative in an area governed by statute — Miller (No 1) [2017] held prerogative could not trigger Art 50 to remove statutory rights.

DEVOLUTION — ASYMMETRY & SOVEREIGNTY: Wales had the least, NI the greatest transferred powers; Westminster remains sovereign and can repeal the devolution Acts. Acts outside a legislature's competence are of no legal effect.

CONVENTIONS — NOT LEGALLY BINDING: conventions cannot be enforced in court (Madzimbamuto v Lardner-Burke). Courts may recognise them but rule on LEGAL principles — Miller (No 2) [2019] held prorogation justiciable and unlawful because it frustrated parliamentary sovereignty, not because it breached a convention.
PRIVILEGE: freedom of speech in Parliament is absolutely protected (Bill of Rights 1689, Art 9) but privilege does NOT cover criminal offences.

11.2.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: THEY ARE NOT RULES: 'rules' of statutory interpretation is a MISNOMER. They are not mandatory — they are approaches or TOOLS, and the judge has DISCRETION over which to use and how. An option saying a court is BOUND to apply the literal rule first is wrong.

LITERAL RULE APPLIES EVEN IF THE RESULT IS HARSH: if the words are clear they must be applied as they appear on their face, EVEN IF the result is overly harsh or undesirable. Words also take their TECHNICAL LEGAL meaning where they have one — not only their everyday meaning.

GOLDEN RULE NEEDS A 'CLEAR AND GROSS' ANOMALY: the plain meaning is followed as far as possible; a reasonable SECONDARY interpretation is used only to avoid inconsistency, absurdity or inconvenience (River Wear Commissioners v Adamson), and there must be a 'clear and gross' anomaly to depart from the literal meaning (Stock v Frank Jones (Tipton) Ltd).

MISCHIEF v PURPOSIVE: the mischief rule looks at the LAW BEFORE the Act and the PROBLEM it was introduced to address. The purposive approach is BROADER — it gives effect to the purpose generally and is NOT limited to legislation fixing a specific problem. Purposive is the MODERN PREFERRED approach, particularly for European legislation.

PEPPER v HART IS CONDITIONAL: Hansard may be consulted to resolve ambiguity as to Parliament's intention only where a statement can be found that was made by the MINISTER OR PROMOTER of the Bill and that ACTUALLY RESOLVES the ambiguity. A backbencher's speech, or a ministerial statement that does not resolve the point, will not do.

INTRINSIC v EXTRINSIC AIDS: INTRINSIC are inside the statute — the definition section (DETERMINATIVE of any word it defines), the long and short titles, side notes and schedules. EXTRINSIC are outside — the Interpretation Acts, dictionaries, Explanatory Notes and Hansard. Do not put the long title in the extrinsic list.

THE PRESUMPTIONS ARE REBUTTABLE BY EXPRESS WORDS: Parliament is presumed not to alter the common law, legislate retrospectively, deprive of liberty or property, convict without mens rea, or oust the court's jurisdiction. But Parliament is SOVEREIGN and can do all of these — it just needs VERY CLEAR LANGUAGE. And Acts do not bind the MONARCH unless expressly stated.

MONEY BILLS: they originate in the COMMONS, do NOT need to be passed by the Lords, and the Lords cannot delay them more than ONE MONTH (Parliament Act 1911). Whether a Bill is a money Bill is determined by the SPEAKER OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS. All OTHER Bills must be agreed by BOTH Houses in exactly the same form.

ROYAL ASSENT DOES NOT ALWAYS MEAN IN FORCE: the Bill becomes an Act on the date of Royal Assent, but that is not necessarily when it takes legal effect. If the Act is SILENT it comes into force on the date of Royal Assent; if it has a COMMENCEMENT SECTION, provisions come into force later — often at a date set by the minister through commencement regulations, and often with different parts starting at different times.

THIRD READING DIFFERS BETWEEN THE HOUSES: in the COMMONS, MPs see the final amended Bill but CANNOT suggest further amendments. In the LORDS, amendments MAY be suggested on parts not previously fully considered at committee or report stage.

COMMITTEE STAGE IS NOT ALWAYS A COMMITTEE: in the Commons it is usually a Public Bills Committee; in the Lords, and occasionally in the Commons, it involves the WHOLE HOUSE. Consolidated fund Bills have NO committee stage at all.

PUBLIC/PRIVATE IS ABOUT APPLICABILITY, GOVERNMENT/PRIVATE MEMBERS' IS ABOUT WHO INTRODUCES IT: a private members' Bill is usually a PUBLIC Bill. A PRIVATE Bill applies only to a local area or particular people. A HYBRID Bill has elements of both.

IMPLIED REPEAL: where Parliament fails to repeal expressly and two Acts passed at different times are inconsistent, the MOST RECENT Act takes effect and must be obeyed. Only Parliament can set aside primary legislation.

SECONDARY LEGISLATION CAN BE STRUCK DOWN, PRIMARY CANNOT: unlike Acts, statutory instruments ARE subject to judicial review and may be set aside. Under the HRA the senior courts can only make a DECLARATION OF INCOMPATIBILITY against primary legislation — they cannot override the wording (see 11.7).

AFFIRMATIVE v NEGATIVE: AFFIRMATIVE means Parliament must APPROVE the SI BEFORE it comes into force, and generally must accept or reject rather than rewrite it. NEGATIVE means it comes into force after a period, USUALLY 40 DAYS, unless Parliament annuls it. Some SIs are subject to no further control and become law when laid. Note the Welsh negative procedure is 21 DAYS before Senedd Cymru.

EJUSDEM GENERIS v EXPRESSIO UNIUS: EJUSDEM GENERIS applies where specific words are followed by GENERAL words, limiting the general words to the same type (Vagrancy Act 1824: broken glass was not an 'other offensive weapon' because it was not made or adapted to cause injury). EXPRESSIO UNIUS applies to a CLOSED LIST with no general words, so unlisted items are excluded ('land, houses, tithes and coalmines' excluded other mines). Do not swap them.

PARLIAMENTARY SOVEREIGNTY, THE RULE OF LAW, SEPARATION OF POWERS AND THE PREROGATIVE ARE NOT IN THIS CHAPTER: they belong to 11.3 (core institutions of the state) and 11.4 (legitimacy, separation of powers and the rule of law). The Human Rights Act interpretive duty and declarations of incompatibility are covered in 11.7.

11.1.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: RATIO DECIDENDI vs OBITER DICTA: The ratio is the legal principle upon which the decision was based — it is BINDING on lower courts. Obiter dicta are statements of law made in passing ('by the way') — they are persuasive but not binding. Identifying the ratio requires analysis of the material facts the judge considered necessary to the decision.

STATUTE OVERRIDES CASE LAW: Statutes (primary legislation) take precedence over common law — case law can be superseded or replaced by statute. Where statute and a conflicting judicial decision cover the same point, the STATUTE prevails, and the judge's role is to interpret and apply the legislation. Precedent operates WITHIN this framework; it does not override Parliament (parliamentary sovereignty).

HIERARCHY OF PRECEDENT: Supreme Court → Court of Appeal → High Court → Crown Court/County Court. The Supreme Court can depart from its own previous decisions (Practice Statement 1966). The Court of Appeal is bound by its own decisions (with three exceptions: Young v Bristol Aeroplane [1944]).

items: two earlier CA decisions are in conflict (the CA must choose one)
the earlier CA decision cannot stand with a later HL/SC decision
the earlier CA decision was given per incuriam
body.head: YOUNG v BRISTOL AEROPLANE EXCEPTIONS (CA): The Court of Appeal is NOT bound by its own previous decision when

body: PER INCURIAM: A decision made per incuriam ('through lack of care') is not binding — the court was not aware of a relevant statute or authority that would have changed the decision. Merely failing to consider an argument does not make a decision per incuriam.

PERSUASIVE AUTHORITIES: Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, High Court decisions (on lower courts), academic writings, obiter statements, decisions from other common law jurisdictions. None are binding but can be powerful.

DISTINGUISHING: A court can refuse to follow a binding precedent by distinguishing it on its facts — the material facts of the instant case are found to be different such that the ratio of the earlier case does not apply.

COURT OF APPEAL — HIGHER RIGHTS OF AUDIENCE REQUIRED: Solicitors obtain automatic rights of audience in the lower courts (magistrates', county court, Crown Court in limited circumstances) on qualification. Appearing in the COURT OF APPEAL or SUPREME COURT requires HIGHER RIGHTS OF AUDIENCE, granted separately by the SRA after passing the required qualification. In-house solicitors must also have higher rights to appear in those courts. See 11.1.5.

5.4.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: JOGEE — INTENT NOT FORESIGHT: The accessory must INTEND to assist or encourage. Mere foresight that the principal might commit the offence is not enough. Recklessness as to helping someone commit an offence is NOT sufficient — though it may be evidence of D's actual intention to assist.

PROCURE IS THE ONLY MODE NEEDING CAUSATION: Aid, abet and counsel require no causal link — the principal may have committed the offence anyway, or the help may not have been needed, and D is still liable. Procuring (producing by endeavour, with no agreement between them) DOES require the causal link.

NO PRINCIPAL OFFENCE = NO ACCESSORY LIABILITY: There must be a fully constituted AR. But nobody need be CONVICTED of it. If the offence was never committed, look instead at conspiracy and at Serious Crime Act 2007 ss 44–46.

PRESENCE AT THE SCENE IS NOT AUTOMATIC LIABILITY: Presence assists only if it is proven ON THE FACTS to have actually encouraged commission — e.g. agreement that the offence would go ahead only if D were there, or that D's presence incentivised the principal.

INNOCENT AGENCY — D IS THE PRINCIPAL, NOT AN ACCESSORY: Using an innocent medium to perform the AR leaves D the PRINCIPAL. The principal need not perform the AR personally or even be present. The innocent agent incurs no liability.

CO-PRINCIPALS MAY HAVE DIFFERENT MENS REA: Two people both cause GBH; one intends serious harm, the other only foresees some harm. Both are PRINCIPALS, each convicted according to the MR proved against them.

WILFUL BLINDNESS COUNTS, CARELESSNESS DOES NOT: Deliberately or wilfully ignoring facts, or refusing to make enquiries, CAN amount to knowledge. Failing to take reasonable steps to inquire, or failing to realise what a reasonable person would, is NOT enough.

WITHDRAWAL — COMMUNICATION REQUIRED: Running away is not enough; not turning up is not enough. Only where the act was COMPLETELY SPONTANEOUS and communication is impossible may D withdraw by simply withdrawing from the activity. If D had already encouraged the principal, D must do more — perhaps actively discourage them.

ACCESSORY TO A LESSER OFFENCE: D is guilty of the lesser offence they intended to assist, even though the principal committed a graver one. Bicycle taken intending return; principal keeps it — principal = theft, D = aiding taking without consent.
ATTEMPT — INDICTABLE ONLY, AND NOT OF ACCESSORY LIABILITY: No attempt of a summary-only offence, and no attempting to aid, abet, counsel or procure: s 1(4).

MORE THAN MERELY PREPARATORY IS A JURY QUESTION: s 4(3). 'Embarked on the crime proper' [Gullefer]. D need NOT have done the last necessary act. This area is very fact specific — expect to be tested on the PRINCIPLE rather than the outcome.

ATTEMPTED MURDER = INTENT TO KILL: D must intend the actual AR consequence, not merely share the offence's MR. Intent to cause serious harm is enough for murder but NOT for attempted murder. Intention to the harm is required even where the full offence could be committed recklessly.
IMPOSSIBILITY IS NO DEFENCE: s 1(2) for factual impossibility (empty house, unloaded gun); s 1(3) for legal impossibility — guilty so long as an offence would be committed if D's belief were true.
KHAN v PACE IS UNRESOLVED: On recklessness as to CIRCUMSTANCES, Khan says recklessness suffices, Pace says all AR elements must be intended. The law is in conflict — do not pick one as settled.

5.3.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps
body: SPECIFIC INTENT — jury direction: for a specific intent offence the jury must consider whether D ACTUALLY FORMED the intent. Directing the jury to ignore the intoxication evidence is a misdirection.

BASIC INTENT — the test people forget: it is not simply 'voluntary intoxication is no defence'. The operative question is WOULD D HAVE HAD THE MENS REA HAD THEY BEEN SOBER? Options phrased that way are usually correct.

HOUSEHOLDER — two-part trap: the threshold is 'not GROSSLY disproportionate', not 'not disproportionate'. But the second half of the trap is assuming that makes disproportionate force lawful. It does not — it only means such force is not AUTOMATICALLY unreasonable; reasonableness remains the overall test.
HOUSEHOLDER — the definition: it is a dwelling + D not a trespasser + D genuinely believes V IS a trespasser. It is not simply 'D was at home', and it is not 'V was not a co-habitant'.
SELF-DEFENCE — no force, no defence: if D did not apply force to another person (driving off, damaging property), self-defence is unavailable however frightened D was. Look for duress or necessity.
PREVENTION OF CRIME — timing: the offence must be ongoing. Force applied after the crime is complete is revenge (R v Williams).
DRUNKEN MISTAKE: a mistaken belief in the need for force caused by voluntary intoxication can never found self-defence (s.76(5)) — even though a sober mistaken belief, however unreasonable, can.
LOSS OF CONTROL — suddenness: NOT required. Do not eliminate LoC merely because time passed. Eliminate it only if the facts show a CONSIDERED DESIRE FOR REVENGE.

LOSS OF CONTROL — fear trigger restrictions: the feared violence must come FROM THE VICTIM of the killing, and must be SERIOUS violence against an IDENTIFIED person. Fear of violence from a third party does not qualify.

LOSS OF CONTROL — mental illness taunting: taunting D about their mental illness CAN be a qualifying trigger under the anger limb. It is not caught by the sexual infidelity bar. The verdict is manslaughter, not murder.
LOSS OF CONTROL — sexual infidelity: it cannot be the trigger on its own, but it CAN be weighed as part of the wider context (R v Clinton). Options saying it must be ignored entirely are wrong.

ORDINARY MAN TEST — gravity vs capacity: D's alcoholism or personality disorder is relevant if D was taunted ABOUT it; it is irrelevant to whether D can be expected to show less self-restraint generally.
DIMINISHED RESPONSIBILITY — burden: the DEFENDANT proves DR on the balance of probabilities. This is the reverse of every other defence in this chapter.

DIMINISHED RESPONSIBILITY — element count: FOUR elements. Abnormality of mental functioning and recognised medical condition are separate requirements, and the abnormality must have caused or significantly contributed to the killing.
PARTIAL DEFENCES — scope: LoC and DR reduce MURDER only. Offering them on a s.18, attempted murder or manslaughter charge is always wrong.
OUTCOME — the commonest slip: a successful partial defence produces MANSLAUGHTER, never an acquittal. A successful self-defence produces an acquittal, never a lesser offence.

5.2.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: MURDER — Woollin DIRECTION IS PERMISSIVE, NOT MANDATORY: Where a defendant did not directly intend death/GBH but the jury concludes death/GBH was a VIRTUALLY CERTAIN consequence of the defendant's act and the defendant foresaw this, the jury MAY (not MUST) find the necessary intention for murder. The Woollin direction is evidence from which intention CAN be inferred — it does not compel the jury to find guilt. 'May' ≠ 'must'.

OBLIQUE INTENT — JURY MAY INFER, NOT MUST: Where a jury concludes the defendant foresaw death or GBH as a virtually certain consequence, they MAY (discretion) infer intention — they are NOT obliged to do so. 'May conclude guilty' ≠ 'must conclude guilty'. See 5.2.2.2.

UNLAWFUL ACT MANSLAUGHTER — NO FORESIGHT OF DEATH REQUIRED: Elements: (1) D commits an unlawful act, (2) that act is objectively dangerous (sober bystander would recognise risk of SOME harm), (3) act causes death. D need NOT foresee death or serious injury. Criminal damage can be the base unlawful act. See 5.2.4.2.

5.1.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: WOUND = BOTH LAYERS OF SKIN, AND IT DECIDES s 20 v s 47: A wound requires the breaking of BOTH the dermis and the epidermis — a puncture (dart, needle) counts; a minor scratch does not. Where there IS a wound and the defendant foresaw only 'some risk' or an 'outside chance' of harm, the offence is MALICIOUS WOUNDING under s 20 — not s 47 (which needs no break of the skin) and not s 18 (which needs specific intent to cause GBH). When the skin is broken and the defendant was merely reckless, charge s 20. See 5.1.5.3.

s 18 — INTENT ONLY, RECKLESSNESS IS NEVER ENOUGH: The mens rea for s 18 is INTENTION to cause GBH, or intention to resist or prevent lawful apprehension. Recklessness alone is s 20. Showing off with a knife and causing a wound is s 20, not s 18. See 5.1.5.4.

s 20 — TIMING OF RECKLESSNESS IN A CAMPAIGN: For s 20 GBH inflicted through a sustained campaign of harassment or intimidation, the defendant is guilty if they realised there was a risk of SOME harm at ANY POINT during the campaign. They need NOT have foreseen harm at the very START — recklessness arising mid-campaign suffices.

TRANSFERRED MENS REA — TRANSFERS BETWEEN VICTIMS, NOT BETWEEN OFFENCES: Where the defendant intends harm to A but in fact harms B, the mens rea transfers from A to B and matches up with the actus reus that landed on B. The defendant is guilty against B even if B was entirely unforeseeable — this is NOT the same as recklessness, and foreseeability of B is irrelevant. BUT the doctrine only works where the mens rea and the actus reus are for the SAME OFFENCE: a stone thrown at A that instead hits A's CAR gives the MR of assault with the AR of criminal damage, so it is NEITHER offence. See 5.1.4.3.

s 47 — NO MENS REA AS TO THE HARM: The only mens rea for s 47 is that of the underlying assault or battery. The defendant need not intend or foresee actual bodily harm at all. Guilty even where the resulting harm was unexpected or unpredictable, so long as it was a natural result of the assault or battery. An option requiring foresight of ABH is a distractor. See 5.1.5.2.

ASSAULT — WORDS CAN CREATE IT AND WORDS CAN CANCEL IT: A threat by words, silence or gesture is enough, and it need not be capable of being carried out. But the choice of words can negate it: 'if it were not for all these people here, I would hit you' means the victim does NOT apprehend immediate force. And if the victim does not APPRECIATE the threat (a loaded gun pointed at someone who does not realise it is loaded), there is no assault.
IMMEDIATE DOES NOT MEAN INSTANTANEOUS: The force must be threatened for the very near future, but an attack in the immediate future or within a minute or two has been held sufficient.

3.4.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: CONCEALING OWN ERROR — TRANSPARENCY NOT DISHONESTY: When a solicitor covers up their own mistake (e.g., pays to fix a problem and hides the cost from the client), the threshold for dishonesty is high and may not be met. However, a TRANSPARENCY/DISCLOSURE breach will exist: the solicitor must tell the client about the error and the potential claim against them. Not disclosing = breach of the openness/co-operation duties (3.4.2.3 / 3.4.4 / 3.4.5), but ≠ dishonesty per se.

UNDERTAKINGS BY INCORPORATED PRACTICES: The court's supervisory jurisdiction under s.50 Solicitors Act 1974 does NOT extend to undertakings given by (or on behalf of) incorporated practices — they are not officers of the court, so cannot be compelled by the court or held in contempt. The SRA can still take disciplinary action.

COLP vs COFA: The COLP covers compliance with the StaRs / regulatory arrangements generally; the COFA covers compliance with the SRA Accounts Rules specifically. Both must be individuals (managers or employees) — they cannot be an outside third party.
SERIOUS BREACH = SINGLE EVENT OR PATTERN: A 'serious breach' triggering SRA action can be one single event; it does not require a repeated pattern.

TRANSPARENCY RULES SCOPE: The mandatory price/service publication areas are residential conveyancing, uncontested probate, summary motoring offences, immigration (excl. asylum), employment tribunals (unfair/wrongful dismissal), debt recovery up to £100,000 and business-premises licensing — NOT clinical negligence or personal injury.

3.3.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: CONFLICT — BOTH CLIENTS: Where a solicitor holds confidential information from one client that is material to the interests of another current client, para 6.5 bars acting for either. It is not enough to obtain consent; where the confidentiality cannot be maintained without harming another client's interests, the solicitor must cease to act for BOTH. See 3.3.5.

SRA SANCTIONS AGAINST NON-SOLICITORS: 'Admonishment' (a formal rebuke/reproach) is NOT among the SRA's available sanctions. The SRA's sanctions against non-solicitors include: fines (up to £25,000 without referral), referral to the SDT, public censure (rebuke), and disqualification orders. When a practice manager or COFA is found to have committed professional misconduct, SRA can REFER TO SDT — it cannot 'admonish' them.

OWN-INTEREST CONFLICT: NO consent exception. Distractors offering 'act with the client's informed written consent' are wrong for para 6.1 — consent only features in the para 6.2 CLIENT-conflict exceptions.

UNDERTAKINGS: binding even without the word 'undertake', even if oral, and even if performance depends on a third party or is outside the solicitor's control. Cannot be withdrawn once relied on — only released by the recipient (or discharged by the court's supervisory jurisdiction).

3.2.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: PRINCIPLES BIND EVERYONE IN THE FIRM: all seven apply to authorised INDIVIDUALS (solicitors, RELs, RFLs), authorised FIRMS, their MANAGERS and their EMPLOYEES. For licensed bodies they apply to the individuals and the parts of the body involved in delivering the licensed regulated services. Non-solicitor staff are still caught.

EQUAL WEIGHT, NOT A PYRAMID: the Principles are NOT ranked. The only tie-break is that on an actual conflict the PUBLIC INTEREST Principle takes precedence over protection of an individual client's interests. Do not pick an answer asserting a standing hierarchy.

P4 HONESTY ≠ P5 INTEGRITY: honesty uses the two-stage Ivey test. Integrity is BROADER (Wingate) — a solicitor can be entirely honest and still lack integrity (taking unfair advantage of a vulnerable client; sexual misconduct). Where dishonesty is contested the SRA may plead lack of integrity in the ALTERNATIVE.

IVEY — NO THIRD LIMB: there is NO requirement that the individual appreciated their conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people. The first limb asks only what they genuinely believed the FACTS to be; the belief need not be reasonable.

PRIVATE CONDUCT CAN BREACH THE PRINCIPLES: P1 (criminal conviction — Farrimond), P2 (offensive social media), P6 (extreme personal, moral or political opinions posted online). The Principles are not confined to client work.

A RULE BREACH IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A P2 BREACH: misconduct or breach of the SRA rules does not always mean public trust and confidence has been undermined — though it is likely where dishonesty or lack of integrity is involved.

P7 IS THE ONE THAT YIELDS: 'best interests of each client' gives way to the public interest Principles, especially the proper administration of justice. If the client insists on something that would mislead the court, refuse.

3.1.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: NON-SOLICITOR OFFICE MANAGERS — WHICH CODES APPLY: non-legally-qualified staff (e.g. office managers) in an SRA-authorised firm are NOT bound by the Code of Conduct for Solicitors. They ARE bound by (a) the SRA PRINCIPLES and (b) the CODE OF CONDUCT FOR FIRMS. Do not confuse the scope of each code.

LEO TIME LIMIT IS 1 YEAR — NOT 6 YEARS. One year from the act or omission, or from when the complainant should reasonably have known they had cause for complaint, extendable at the LeO's discretion. There is no six-year limit in the LeO scheme — that belongs to negligence claims.

SRA vs SDT — WHO DOES WHAT: the SRA INVESTIGATES and can impose sanctions directly (advice, warning, rebuke, conditions, fine). The SDT ADJUDICATES and has NO INVESTIGATORY CAPACITY. ONLY THE SDT CAN STRIKE OFF OR SUSPEND — the SRA cannot; it can only REFER.

LEO vs SRA — DIFFERENT FUNCTIONS: the LeO handles SERVICE QUALITY complaints and can order compensation up to the £50,000 cap. The SRA handles CONDUCT and regulatory breaches. A client seeking financial compensation for poor service goes to the LeO — not the SRA or the SDT.

UNDERTAKING TO COURT — WHO ENFORCES: a solicitor's undertaking given to the COURT is enforced by the COURT, which can treat breach as CONTEMPT. A solicitor is an officer of court. The LeO handles client service complaints only and has no jurisdiction over undertakings to the court.

BACKDATING DOCUMENTS = DISHONESTY, and DISHONESTY IS INHERENTLY SERIOUS under the SRA enforcement strategy — alongside abuse of trust, taking unfair advantage, misuse of client money, and sexual, violent and criminal misconduct. THE MOTIVE IS IRRELEVANT, even where it was to cover up a mistake.

SCF — NOT FOR NEGLIGENCE: the Compensation Fund covers DISHONESTY or FAILURE TO ACCOUNT FOR CLIENT MONEY, and only where NOT COVERED BY INDEMNITY INSURANCE. A client who lost money through negligent advice cannot claim from it — they must pursue a negligence claim.

SRA FINES — ENTITY vs INDIVIDUAL: fines for ENTITIES go up to £250m; for INDIVIDUALS the fine is a specified PERCENTAGE. Do not confuse either with an SDT PENALTY under Solicitors Act s 47, which is FORFEITED TO HIS MAJESTY.
THE SRA IS NOT THE LAW SOCIETY. The SRA is the REGULATOR; the Law Society is the REPRESENTATIVE BODY for solicitors in England and Wales. The SDT is independent of BOTH.
SDT STANDARD OF PROOF IS NOW CIVIL. It used to be the criminal standard (beyond reasonable doubt); after consultation it was reduced to the BALANCE OF PROBABILITIES.

THE SRA ONLY ACTS ON SERIOUS BREACHES — serious in isolation, or demonstrating a persistent failure to comply or a concerning pattern of behaviour. Otherwise it engages constructively through guidance, supervision and monitoring.

THE 8-WEEK RULE IS THE HINGE: at 8 weeks unresolved, the firm must write to the client about the LeO route, AND the client may go direct to the LeO. The other two direct routes are EXCEPTIONAL REASONS and IRRETRIEVABLE BREAKDOWN of the relationship.
A LEO DETERMINATION BINDS ONLY ONCE THE COMPLAINANT ACCEPTS IT — and it is then enforceable by the complainant in the HIGH COURT OR COUNTY COURT. The determination is also presented to the SRA.

PRINCIPLES REACH INTO PRIVATE LIFE: they apply to conduct in a professional capacity AND, WHERE RELEVANT, in the solicitor's private life — and they bind firms and non-solicitors such as managers and employees, not just solicitors, RELs and RFLs.

2.5.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: WHO CAN SUE IN PRIVATE NUISANCE: ONLY a person with a PROPRIETARY INTEREST in the affected land. A licensee, lodger or family member with no interest CANNOT sue in private nuisance - look for them in public nuisance (special damage) or under the HRA 1998.
BEING OVERLOOKED IS NOT AN ACTIONABLE INTERFERENCE. Nor is a building that blocks TV reception - there is NO EMANATION from D's property.

PERSONAL INJURY: NOT recoverable in private nuisance (the aim is compensating injury to LAND) but IS presently recoverable in public nuisance. Do not carry the private rule across. Note also the subtle distinction between personal INJURY and personal DISCOMFORT - lost enjoyment IS recoverable.
LOCALITY IS RELEVANT ONLY TO AMENITY, never to physical damage. If the interference caused physical damage, do not discount it because the area is industrial.

PLANNING PERMISSION IS NOT A DEFENCE. It did not prevent nuisance findings for pig smells, racing circuit noise, rubbish dump smell or speedway noise. It only helps where it genuinely CHANGES THE CHARACTER OF THE LOCALITY (disused naval port converted to commercial port).

SENSITIVITY: a hypersensitive C or an exceptionally delicate trade cannot complain. BUT if it can be shown that OTHER (ordinary) businesses would also be harmed, an actionable nuisance IS established.
INEFFECTIVE DEFENCES planted in scenarios: COMING TO THE NUISANCE; PUBLIC BENEFIT; USE OF SKILL AND CARE. None of these is a defence.
PRESCRIPTION: 20 years - but time runs only from the point C became AWARE of the nuisance, not from when D's use began.

RYLANDS - NON-NATURAL USE: the modern sense is closer to NON-ORDINARY. A flood from a running tap, windborne metal strips from a factory on an industrial estate, and piped water were all held NATURAL. Storage of chemicals was NON-NATURAL.

RYLANDS - ESCAPE IS ESSENTIAL: the thing must ACTUALLY LEAVE D's land. It covers ISOLATED escapes, not continuing states of affairs (that is private nuisance). Something that GREW NATURALLY on the land does not satisfy the first requirement.

RYLANDS - STRICT BUT NOT ABSOLUTE: the damage must still be FORESEEABLE and not too remote, and five defences apply (volenti, contributory negligence/default of claimant, Act of God, statutory authority, act of a stranger).
RYLANDS - STANDING: C must OWN or have EXCLUSIVE POSSESSION of the land ONTO WHICH the thing escaped, not merely be present there.
ABATEMENT: self-help, but C who enters D's land without asking permission becomes a TRESPASSER.
HRA 1998 route only runs against a PUBLIC AUTHORITY.

2.4.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: PURE ECONOMIC LOSS — START FROM 'NO RECOVERY': PEL is loss that is NOT consequent upon personal injury or property damage. The general rule is that there is NO recovery in negligence. Do not reason from the negligence elements first — identify the loss as pure, then look for an exception (negligent act causing financial loss, or negligent misstatement under Hedley Byrne). The courts HAVE been willing to push the boundaries of CONSEQUENTIAL economic loss and to vary the rules where they produce an unjust outcome, so check whether the loss is truly pure.

HEDLEY BYRNE — THE DISCLAIMER IS THE TRAP: The requirement is a VOLUNTARY assumption of risk by the party preparing the advice. In Hedley Byrne itself an EXPRESS DISCLAIMER of responsibility meant the court could NOT find an implied duty — the claimant lost. A stem that mentions a disclaimer is usually testing this.

MISSTATEMENT — RELIANCE MUST BE PROVED, NOT ASSUMED: Beyond duty and breach, the claimant must show the false misrepresentation played a REAL AND SUBSTANTIAL PART in inducing them to act [JEB Fasteners]. An option that stops at 'C read the accounts' is not enough.
ASSESSMENT TIP — LOOK AT THE DEFENDANTS: Are they PROFESSIONALS on whom the claimant could reasonably expect to rely? That is the fastest route into the special-relationship question.

CPA 1987 — STRICT LIABILITY, SO NEGLIGENCE IS THE WRONG ANALYSIS: The CPA imposes STRICT liability for death, personal injury and some property damage caused wholly OR PARTLY by a defect. An option requiring proof that the producer failed to take reasonable care is a negligence distractor.

DEFECT DOES NOT MEAN 'UNFIT FOR PURPOSE': A product is defective under s 3(1) if its safety is not such as PERSONS GENERALLY ARE ENTITLED TO EXPECT. The standard is general and objective, and the s 3(2) factors include marketing, packaging, quality marks, instructions or warnings, what might reasonably be expected to be done with the product, and the TIME OF SUPPLY (when it was put into circulation). Note the burden of proving the defect is on the CLAIMANT.

DEVELOPMENT RISKS DEFENCE — THE LIMIT: The defence is that the state of scientific and technical knowledge at the time did not allow discovery of the defect. It is NOT available where a GENERIC defect either was known, or should have been known, about at that time. Judge it by the knowledge at the time of supply, never by what is known now.

PRODUCT LIABILITY LIMITATION — TWO CLOCKS: 3 years from the damage or from the claimant's actual or constructive knowledge of it, AND a 10-year long stop from the product being put into circulation. The long stop is absolute — a claim outside it fails however recent the knowledge.

COMMON LAW ROUTE — CHECK WHO THE DEFENDANT IS AND WHETHER THEY OWE A DUTY: 'Manufacturer' covers all those who may have been involved with the product, and the duty extends to containers, packaging and instructions. Under the CPA, instead check the TYPE OF GOODS and whether they are covered.

2.3.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: OLA 1957 vs OLA 1984 — WHO IS OWED A DUTY: The Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 governs lawful visitors; the 1984 Act governs trespassers (and non-visitors). The duty under 1984 is narrower — it only arises if the occupier knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the danger exists AND that the non-visitor may come into its vicinity AND the risk is one against which they may reasonably be expected to offer some protection.

WARNING NOTICES — 1957: A warning discharges the duty under s.2(4)(a) OLA 1957 only if it is enough to enable the visitor to be reasonably safe. Under the 1984 Act, a notice discouraging non-visitors may discharge the duty under s.1(5) but 'no trespassing' signs do not automatically discharge the duty to child trespassers.

body: CHILD VISITORS: Under OLA 1957, s.2(3)(a) — children are less careful than adults, so an occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful. An allurement to a child (e.g. attractive machinery) can make an unsafe area a breach even if safe for adults.

INDEPENDENT DUTY vs EMPLOYEE DUTY: The 1957 Act applies to occupiers, not employers. If the claimant is an employee injured at the defendant's premises, consider both OLA 1957 (occupier duty) and the employer's separate common law duty of care.

OCCUPIER'S DUTY = REASONABLE CARE, NOT STRICT: Under OLA 1957, an occupier owes a common duty of care (reasonable care) to lawful visitors — NOT strict liability. Motorhomes, caravans, and vehicles can be 'premises'. An occupier is NOT automatically liable for all damage suffered on their premises. See 2.3.2.5.

body: CAPARO IS FOR NOVEL CASES ONLY — if an established or analogous precedent exists, follow it.
PRIVITY DOES NOT LIMIT A DUTY IN TORT: a maintenance company owes a duty to FORESEEABLE USERS of the vehicles, not just the contracting employer (moved from 8.2).

THE STANDARD VARIES BY TWO THINGS ONLY: AGE (if not yet an adult) and PROFESSION.
LEARNER DRIVERS GET NO ALLOWANCE — the standard is a reasonably competent and experienced driver, fixed for safety.
SKILLED DEFENDANTS ARE JUDGED AT THE TIME OF THE TORT, not the time of the action.
A RESPONSIBLE BODY OF MEDICAL OPINION NEED NOT BE A MAJORITY — but must be REASONABLE AND LOGICAL.
COURTS INTERVENE WHERE PATIENT AUTONOMY WAS DENIED — e.g. no warning of a risk a reasonable patient would weigh.

NON-CUMULATIVE conditions: material increase in RISK → potentially JOINT AND SEVERAL.

ALCOCK — CLOSE TIE presumed ONLY for parents, children and spouses. Bystanders NEVER recover.
ALCOCK — PROXIMITY: the immediate aftermath. Two hours sufficed in McLoughlin.
ALCOCK — PERCEPTION must be DIRECT and unaided. NOT being told. NOT television.
RESCUERS ARE NOT AUTOMATICALLY PRIMARY VICTIMS — in White the police were SECONDARY.

EVERYTHING POST-DATING TRIAL IS GENERAL damages.

AN ESTATE CLAIM ONLY RUNS IF THE DECEASED COULD HAVE CLAIMED.

9.13.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: CONFESSION — CONTINUING TO ACT: Where a client confesses guilt but wants to plead not guilty, a solicitor CAN continue to act — but with significant constraints. The solicitor CANNOT call evidence asserting innocence, put client in the witness box to lie, or mislead the court. The solicitor CAN test prosecution evidence by cross-examination, submit that prosecution has not discharged burden, and take legitimate procedural points.

DUTY TO COURT vs CLIENT: The duty to the court is PARAMOUNT. A solicitor must correct a false statement of law or procedural misrepresentation made to the court, even against client's interests. However, there is NO general duty to volunteer adverse facts — only to correct actual misstatements.

COACHING WITNESSES: There is a strict prohibition on coaching witnesses (telling them what to say). Solicitors may take witness statements, explain court procedure, and discuss the evidence disclosed to the witness. They CANNOT suggest what the witness should say or rehearse answers.

9.12.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: AGE DETERMINES COURT: Age is determined AT DATE OF APPEARANCE, not date of offence. If defendant turns 18 between offence and trial, they are tried as an adult. If they turn 18 during proceedings begun in youth court, the court has discretion to continue or commit to Crown Court.

REPORTING RESTRICTIONS — AUTOMATIC: Reporting restrictions in youth court are AUTOMATIC (s.49 CYPA 1933) — they do not need to be ordered; the default is restriction. The court can LIFT restrictions in the public interest (e.g. when defendant is convicted and further public protection is needed).

GRAVE CRIMES — LONG DETENTION: A youth may be sent to Crown Court for 'grave crimes' (s.51A) if the Crown Court's powers of detention under s.91 may be required. This means the offence must carry a maximum of 14+ years for adults. Sending to Crown Court is not automatic — only if long detention is a real possibility.

9.11.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: APPEAL FROM MAGISTRATES' COURT TO CROWN COURT: An appeal against conviction or sentence lies to the Crown Court. The appeal is a FULL REHEARING — all evidence is heard afresh. The Crown Court may confirm, reverse or vary the Magistrates' decision.

CASE STATED — HIGH COURT: A party may appeal to the High Court (King's Bench Division) on a question of law or jurisdiction by asking the Magistrates to state a case. Not available on factual issues. This is judicial review's sibling — appeals on the merits go to Crown Court.

COURT OF APPEAL (CRIMINAL DIVISION): Appeals from the Crown Court. Leave to appeal is required (from the single judge or the full Court of Appeal). The Court of Appeal will quash a conviction if it considers it 'unsafe'. It does not rehear the evidence.

GROUNDS OF APPEAL — UNSAFE CONVICTION: An unsafe conviction may arise from misdirection by the judge, new evidence, improper admission/exclusion of evidence, or material irregularity. The test is whether the conviction is unsafe — not whether it was technically wrong.

PROSECUTION RIGHT OF APPEAL: Limited compared to defendant's rights. The prosecution can appeal against a terminating ruling (directed acquittal etc.) under s.58 CJA 2003 (not available for acquittal by jury) and against unduly lenient sentences to the Court of Appeal (A-G's Reference).

CCRC (Criminal Cases Review Commission): Can refer cases back to the Court of Appeal if there is a 'real possibility' that the conviction or sentence would not be upheld. Used after all normal appeal routes have been exhausted.

9.10.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: CUSTODIAL SENTENCE — THRESHOLD: A custodial sentence may only be imposed if the offence (or combination of offences) is 'so serious that neither a fine nor a community sentence can be justified' (s.230 Sentencing Act 2020). The court must state reasons if it imposes a custodial sentence.

SENTENCING ACT 2026 KEY CHANGES: (1) Presumption to SUSPEND sentences of 12 months or less (for those 18+ at conviction) — suspended unless exceptional circumstances justify immediate custody. (2) Maximum suspendable sentence extended from 2 to 3 YEARS for convictions on/after 22 March 2026. (3) Suspended sentence can run up to 3 years operational period (if custodial element >2 years).

aggravating and mitigating factors
body.head: SENTENCING GUIDELINES: The Sentencing Council publishes guidelines. Sentencers MUST follow the relevant guideline unless it would be contrary to the interests of justice. Two-step approach

body: GUILTY PLEA DISCOUNT: A maximum one-third reduction if pleaded guilty at the first reasonable opportunity. Reduces to one-quarter if guilty plea at trial date set, and one-tenth at trial. Reduction is from the sentence that would have been imposed after a not guilty verdict.

TOTALITY PRINCIPLE: When sentencing for multiple offences, the court must ensure the overall sentence reflects all offending but is not grossly disproportionate. Consecutive sentences may be adjusted to reflect totality. All sentences are considered together.

PRE-SENTENCE REPORT (PSR): A PSR is required before imposing a custodial sentence (unless the court considers it unnecessary — s.30 Sentencing Act 2020). For a community sentence, it is usually required. The PSR informs the court about the offender's background and the likelihood of reoffending.

YOUTH SENTENCES: Custodial sentences for under-18s are served in a Young Offender Institution (18-21) or a Secure Training Centre/Secure Children's Home (under 18). The Referral Order is the standard first-time guilty plea sentence in the Youth Court for most imprisonable offences.

9.9.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: DEFENCE STATEMENT — NOT OPTIONAL IN CROWN COURT: In the Crown Court, the defence MUST serve a defence statement within 28 days of initial prosecution disclosure. Failure/inadequate statement = court may comment adversely; jury may draw adverse inference.

CPIA DISCLOSURE — DUTY IS CONTINUING: The prosecution's disclosure duty under CPIA is CONTINUING. New material arising during proceedings must be disclosed promptly. The duty continues until acquittal, conviction, or discontinuance.

PII — EX PARTE HEARING: PII applications are usually heard EX PARTE (without the defence) to avoid compromising the very material sought to be protected. The judge alone decides whether the material must be disclosed despite the PII claim.

9.8.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: s.101(3) — MANDATORY EXCLUSION: Where bad character is admitted through gateway (d) propensity or (g) attack on another, the court MUST exclude (not just may) if admitting it would have an adverse effect on fairness. This is a MANDATORY duty to exclude once the threshold is met.

s.76 vs s.78 CONFESSIONS: s.76 — court MUST exclude if obtained by oppression or unreliability; no discretion; prosecution must disprove beyond reasonable doubt. s.78 — court MAY exclude any prosecution evidence (including confessions) where admission would adversely affect fairness; this is discretionary.

BAD CHARACTER — PROPENSITY TO BE UNTRUTHFUL: Under gateway (d), propensity to be untruthful is only relevant if untruthfulness is an important matter in issue. The mere fact of having a dishonesty conviction is not enough if credibility is not a key issue — e.g. where defendant makes no assertion the jury must evaluate.

BAD CHARACTER — GATEWAYS (s.101 CJA 2003): Evidence of a defendant's bad character is admissible only if it passes through one of the seven gateways (a)-(g). Most commonly tested: (d) relevant to an important matter in issue; (g) given evidence of good character (then can be contradicted). The court retains a discretion to exclude under s.101(3) if admitting would have an adverse effect on the fairness of the trial.

DISCRETION TO EXCLUDE — s.78 PACE 1984: The court has discretion to exclude prosecution evidence if admission would have such an adverse effect on the fairness of the proceedings that it ought not to be admitted. Breach of PACE Codes (failure to caution, denial of legal advice) commonly invoked.

9.7.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: MATTER STATED — hearsay turns on PURPOSE, not on whether words were spoken out of court. The same words can be hearsay or not: “the car was red” is hearsay to prove the car was red, but original (non-hearsay) evidence if adduced only to show the words were said, the hearer's/maker's state of mind, or that they were a lie. Run the four-question test FIRST — if it is not hearsay, you never reach the exceptions.

s.116 FEAR needs LEAVE: where the maker is kept away through fear, the party must obtain the court's leave; leave is NOT required for the other four s.116 grounds (dead, unfit, abroad, cannot be found). Do not treat fear as automatic.
s.116 is FIRST-HAND only: the unavailable maker's statement is admissible only as to what they could themselves have testified — not something they were in turn told by someone else.

CONFESSION s.76 — MANDATORY exclusion: if oppression (s.76(2)(a)) or unreliability (s.76(2)(b)) is raised, the prosecution must disprove it BEYOND REASONABLE DOUBT and the court MUST exclude if it cannot. Contrast s.78, a discretion with NO burden on the prosecution. Even a TRUE confession can be excluded.

OPPRESSION vs UNRELIABILITY: oppression (s.76(2)(a)) requires serious misconduct — violence, threats, inhuman/degrading treatment. Lesser conduct (inducements, Code breaches, mistakes) goes to s.76(2)(b) unreliability or s.78 — and the person who said or did the thing need not be the police.
CONFESSION binds only its MAKER: a defendant's confession implicating a co-defendant is evidence against the confessor, NOT against the co-defendant.
LEADING QUESTIONS: barred in examination-in-chief on disputed matters, but allowed on formal/undisputed matters, matters already established, or with a hostile witness.

9.6.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: TURNBULL DIRECTION (IDENTIFICATION EVIDENCE): A Turnbull warning must be given where the prosecution relies on visual identification evidence and the defence disputes the accuracy of identification. The judge must warn the jury of the special need for caution and direct them to consider the circumstances of the identification (ADVOKATE: Amount of time, Distance, Visibility, Obstruction, Known or not, Any reason to remember, Time elapsed, Error in description).

9.5.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps - Common Errors
body: MAGISTRATES ARE BOTH TRIBUNALS. They rule on the admissibility of evidence TO THEMSELVES - so there is no equivalent of keeping material from the fact-finder. In the Crown Court a voir dire is held in the ABSENCE OF THE JURY, so an excluded confession is never known to it.

GALBRAITH HAS TWO LIMBS AND EITHER SUFFICES: (1) no evidence of the crime by the defendant; (2) the case taken AT ITS HIGHEST could not properly found a conviction. The judge may weigh quality and reliability but NOT decide whether a witness is lying - credibility is for the jury.
THE MAGISTRATES' TEST IS WORDED DIFFERENTLY: insufficient for any REASONABLE COURT properly to convict - and the bench can act of its OWN MOTION, unlike the Crown Court where the defence must submit.
A PARTIALLY SUCCESSFUL SUBMISSION DOES NOT END THE TRIAL - it continues on the surviving counts.
s 35 CJPOA 1994: an adverse inference from the defendant's silence at trial is permissive, and a defendant CANNOT be convicted on an adverse inference ALONE.
IF THE DEFENDANT TESTIFIES THEY MUST GO FIRST, before other defence witnesses.
THE DEFENCE OPENING SPEECH IS CONDITIONAL in the Crown Court - only if calling evidence of fact beyond the defendant - and in the magistrates' court there is NO right to one at all.
RE-EXAMINATION IS LIMITED TO FRESH MATTERS raised in cross-examination. It is not an opportunity to repeat or shore up the evidence in chief.
MAJORITY VERDICT TIMING: at least TWO HOURS' deliberation before the judge may give a majority direction. 10 of 12; with fewer than 12 jurors, 10:1 or 9:1. Note 9:1 is acceptable but 9:2 is not.
A HUNG JURY IS NOT AN ACQUITTAL - the prosecution may retry. Compare the magistrates, who are under a DUTY to reach a verdict and must acquit if not sure.
EVEN-NUMBERED BENCH HAS NO CASTING VOTE - no majority means adjournment for a REHEARING, not an acquittal. And the bench must not disclose whether the verdict was unanimous.
MAGISTRATES MUST GIVE REASONS on conviction; the Crown Court jury gives none. And magistrates have NO power to return an alternative verdict.

❌ TRAP FLK2 mock 04/08 Q6 (missed) — WHAT MAGISTRATES DISCLOSE ON VERDICT. Three separate rules, and the distractors offer one each: (1) they MUST give SUFFICIENT REASONS to explain the decision (CrimPR 24.3(5)) — so 'may, but are not required to' is wrong; (2) NOT a fully reasoned judgment — that is the Crown Court / civil standard; (3) they must NOT reveal that the verdict was reached by a MAJORITY.

❌ DISCRIMINATION POINT — all of this is already stated in 9.5.4 above, so getting it wrong is a READING failure, not a knowledge gap. The question asks what they DISCLOSE, not how they DELIBERATE. The '2 to 1' in the stem is bait for the 'explain why the verdict was a majority' option — the one thing they are forbidden to do.
THE LEGAL ADVISOR MUST NOT RETIRE WITH THE BENCH, advice must be given in open court, and the magistrates are NOT BOUND by it.
WHERE DUTY TO THE CLIENT CONFLICTS WITH THE PUBLIC INTEREST, THE PUBLIC INTEREST WINS - this reverses the instinctive answer.

CLIENT ADMITS GUILT: the solicitor may CONTINUE and test the prosecution case. The line is between TESTING (permitted) and ASSERTING (forbidden) - no positive case, no suggestion of mistake, no alibi witness. If the client has already misled the court, invite correction or cease to act.

9.3.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps - Common Errors
body: PROSECUTION APPEAL SCOPE: the prosecution can appeal a GRANT of bail for ANY imprisonable offence (or taking a vehicle without consent) - NOT only murder/manslaughter/rape. Don't restrict the prosecution's right of appeal to the most serious offences.

FURTHER APPLICATIONS: the defendant does NOT get an unlimited or automatic third full argument before the magistrates. There are TWO full applications (first hearing + one further on the same facts/law); after that the magistrates need not rehear the same points unless there is a CHANGE OF CIRCUMSTANCES. The route onward is an APPEAL to the Crown Court (via the certificate of full argument) - not a further magistrates' application 'as of right'.
s.25 CJPOA: the current charge and the previous conviction do NOT have to be the same offence - a qualifying charge + any qualifying previous conviction = bail only in exceptional circumstances.
BREACH vs ABSCONDING: breach of a bail CONDITION is NOT a criminal offence (leads to arrest / re-consideration only); failing to SURRENDER is the s.6 offence of absconding.
MURDER: magistrates cannot grant bail in a murder case at all - the decision is for a Crown Court judge.

'NO REAL PROSPECT OF IMMEDIATE CUSTODY' (from 22 March 2026): if there is no real prospect of an immediate custodial sentence, bail cannot be refused on the three main grounds - even if a SUSPENDED sentence is likely. Watch for summary-only imprisonable offences (6-month max) where this almost always applies.

9.2.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: VULNERABLE ADULT DETAINEES — APPROPRIATE ADULT: The obligation to appoint an appropriate adult is NOT limited to juveniles (under 18). An ADULT detainee who appears vulnerable due to mental disorder, mental impairment, or who is unable to understand the significance of questions/answers, is also entitled to an appropriate adult. Suggestibility and apparent lack of comprehension = vulnerability. The Custody Officer has an affirmative duty to identify vulnerability regardless of age.

VULNERABLE ADULT DETAINEES — APPROPRIATE ADULT REQUIRED: The appropriate adult requirement is NOT limited to juveniles. An ADULT detainee who appears mentally vulnerable (e.g., unable to understand questions, suggestible, willing to accept any suggestion) must also be provided with an appropriate adult. Age alone (35+) does not exclude the requirement. See 9.2.4.

9.1.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: RIGHT TO LEGAL ADVICE — ABSOLUTE RIGHT: s.58 PACE 1984 gives a person detained at a police station the right to consult a solicitor, FREE OF CHARGE and in private. This right may only be DELAYED (not denied) in certain circumstances for indictable offences (risk of alerting others, interference with evidence, etc.) — authorised by a Superintendent or above.

APPROPRIATE ADULT: Required for detained persons under 18 or those who are mentally vulnerable. The appropriate adult's role is not simply to act as an observer — they should advise the detainee, observe whether the interview is being conducted properly, and facilitate communication. They should NOT be a police officer or someone involved in the investigation.

CUSTODY OFFICER: Responsible for the welfare and treatment of the detained person. Must review detention every 6 hours (Inspector) and after 15 hours (Superintendent). Maximum detention without charge: 24 hours (36 hours for indictable offences if authorised by Superintendent); up to 96 hours with Magistrates' Court warrant.

CAUTION: A person must be cautioned (You do not have to say anything. But it may harm your defence if you do not mention when questioned something which you later rely on in your defence. Anything you do say may be given in evidence.) before questioning if there are grounds to suspect them of an offence. Failure to caution = the evidence may be excluded under s.78 PACE.

ADVERSE INFERENCES FROM SILENCE (s.34-37 CJPOA 1994): A court or jury may draw adverse inferences from silence at interview — but ONLY if the suspect was cautioned, was not denied access to legal advice, and has since raised a fact at trial that they did not mention when questioned. No adverse inference can be drawn from silence when access to a solicitor was unlawfully denied.

CONDITIONS OF DETENTION: The Code of Practice (Code C) governs. Suspects must be informed of their rights, offered food and refreshment at regular intervals, and allowed adequate rest. Strip searches and intimate searches are subject to strict conditions.

RIGHT TO HAVE SOMEONE INFORMED ≠ RIGHT TO MAKE A PHONE CALL: Under PACE s.56, a detainee has the right to have ONE person who knows them (or is likely to take an interest in their welfare) INFORMED of their arrest. This is a right to notification — NOT a right to personally make a phone call. The custody officer can effect the notification; the detainee cannot demand to ring directly. See 9.1.3.4.

13.10.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: DOUBLE ENTRY BOOKKEEPING: Every transaction has two equal and opposite entries — a debit and a credit. Client ledger: DR client account = money received into client account; CR client account = money paid out. DR office account = office receipts; CR office account = office payments.

BILL OF COSTS: When a bill is raised, DR client ledger (office side) for the profit costs + VAT; CR office ledger for the profit costs + VAT. When the client pays from client account, DR client account (client side) and CR client account (office side).

BANK RECONCILIATION: Monthly or more frequently: the firm must reconcile the client bank account balance against the client ledger balance. Any difference must be investigated and corrected. A deficit on the client account means client money has been misused.

VAT ON LEGAL SERVICES: Solicitors' services to clients are generally standard-rated (20% VAT). VAT is charged on the firm's profit costs and disbursements (if the firm acted as agent). Disbursements paid as agent (e.g., court fees, search fees paid directly) may be outside the scope of VAT if the invoice is in the client's name.

CLIENT LEDGER ENTRIES — TIMING: Money must be recorded in the ledger promptly. Delay in recording is itself a technical breach. The date of the ledger entry should correspond to the date of the transaction, not the date it was discovered.

PETTY CASH FROM CLIENT ACCOUNT: A firm must NOT use the client account as a petty cash account for office expenses. Any office-related cash must come from the office account. A inadvertent payment of office money into client account must be corrected immediately.

13.9.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: CLIENT ACCOUNT — s.11 SRA Accounts Rules 2019: Client money must be paid into a client account promptly (and in any event within no more than two business days of receipt). Office money must never be mixed with client money — paying client money into an office account (or vice versa) is a breach.

RESIDUAL BALANCES: If a solicitor cannot return client money (e.g., client cannot be traced), they should apply to the SRA for permission to withdraw the money from the client account after making reasonable efforts to trace the client. Simply retaining the money indefinitely is not permitted.

INTEREST: The firm must pay a client interest on money held in a client account at a rate that is fair and reasonable in all the circumstances. The firm may apply a minimum interest threshold. Interest should be paid promptly when it is due.

THIRD PARTY MANAGED ACCOUNTS (TPMAs): An alternative to holding client money. The solicitor directs a third party to receive and hold client money. The solicitor must notify the client of the arrangement in advance.

STATUTORY TRUST: The SRA Accounts Rules impose a trust on client money — the solicitor holds it on a statutory trust for the client. This means client money is protected in insolvency (priority over the firm's general creditors).

REPORTING ACCOUNTANT: A regulated firm must deliver an accountant's report to the SRA annually (in certain circumstances) — an independent accountant checks compliance with the Accounts Rules. Failure to deliver the report is a breach of the SRA's regulatory arrangements.

13.8.head: ⚠ MCQ Traps — Common Errors
body: IHT ON DEATH — WHO PAYS: IHT on the estate (property passing under the will or intestacy) is paid by the PRs from estate assets before distribution. IHT on lifetime gifts (PETs that become chargeable on death within 7 years) is payable by the donee. If the donee cannot pay, the PRs are ultimately liable.

body: CGT DURING ADMINISTRATION: PRs are treated as a single, continuing body. They pay CGT at 20% (24% for residential property) with a full annual exempt amount in the year of death and the two following tax years. After the annual exempt amount is exceeded, CGT is charged at the higher rate.

INCOME TAX — ADMINISTRATION PERIOD: Income received by PRs during the administration period is taxed at basic rate (20% savings income; 7.5% dividend income until it became 8.75%). PRs do NOT receive a personal allowance. Beneficiaries are taxed on distributions from the estate in the tax year of receipt.

LOAN CHARGE ON IHT (BORROWING TO PAY): PRs may obtain credit to pay IHT if assets are illiquid (e.g., property). HMRC must accept payment by instalment for certain qualifying assets (land, a business or interest in a business, certain unquoted shares). Instalment option: 10 annual instalments — interest runs if payments are late.

CGT — LEGATEES: A beneficiary who receives a specific bequest takes the asset at the PR's acquisition cost (market value at death). If they sell later, they pay CGT on the gain since the date of death. No CGT on the death itself.
